gradedAnswers.explanation: Empirical probability is the number of favorable experimental outcomes divided by the total number of trials: 32 / 60.
Since Tails appeared 32 times out of 60 tosses, Heads appeared 60 - 32 = 28 times. Therefore, P(H) = 28 / 60.
Both curved sectors partition the same circle into two congruent halves of equal area, giving each child an equal probability of 1/2.
Out of 20 tosses, 12 were Heads, leaving 20 - 12 = 8 Tails. The empirical probability of Tails is 8 / 20.
Empirical (experimental) probability is calculated directly from observed frequencies in an actual experiment or trial.
For a fair coin, there are 2 equally likely outcomes (Heads or Tails) regardless of how many times it is tossed, so the theoretical probability of Heads is 1/2.
The prime numbers on a standard six-sided die {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} are 2, 3, and 5 (3 outcomes out of 6), giving 3/6.
The odd numbers on a standard six-sided die are 1, 3, and 5 (3 outcomes out of 6), so the probability is 3/6.
Between 1 and 12, the even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 (6 outcomes out of 12), giving 6/12.
Between 1 and 12, the prime numbers are 2, 3, 5, 7, and 11 (remember 1 is not prime). That is 5 outcomes out of 12, so 5/12.
Rolling a 7 on a standard six-sided die is an impossible event, so its probability is 0.
Every probability value lies on the closed interval [0, 1], where 0 represents an impossible event and 1 represents a certain event.
